parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how an analogue speech wave looks compared to what can travel cleanly down an optic fibre - is it continuously varying or jumping between just two fixed levels?
parts.proper_answer: A digital signal consists of a series of 1s and 0s (high and low voltages / ons and offs), with only discrete values and no intermediate values.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Analogue Versus Digital**
Think of your voice as a smooth, continuously changing air pressure wave. An analogue voltage copy of it can take any value. For reliable long-distance transmission we do not want that. We want something much simpler that noise cannot easily corrupt.

Step 2: **Define the Digital Form**
That simpler form uses just two levels. So a digital signal is a sequence of pulses representing binary 1 and 0, for example +5 V for 1 and 0 V for 0. There is nothing in between.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Follow the signal path in Fig. 3.1 - the ADC outputs several bits at once in parallel, but the fibre can only carry one bit at a time, so what must X do? At the far end after parallel is restored, what must Y do to drive a loudspeaker?
Hint 2: Recall the symmetry of the system: ADC changes analogue to digital at the start, so the reverse block is needed at the end before amplification to the speaker.
parts.proper_answer: X: parallel-to-serial converter. Y: DAC / digital-to-analogue converter.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why X Is Needed Before the Fibre**
The ADC produces, say, an 8-bit number for each sample with all 8 bits available at the same time on 8 wires. An optic fibre carries a single stream of pulses. So X must line those bits up one after another. That is a parallel-to-serial converter.

Step 2: **Why Y Is Needed After the Fibre**
At the receiver the serial-to-parallel converter restores the parallel 8-bit numbers. The loudspeaker needs a continuously varying analogue voltage, not numbers. So Y must rebuild an analogue voltage from each digital number. That is a DAC, a digital-to-analogue converter.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: The input to the ADC from the microphone amplifier is still a smooth analogue voltage - how could you capture its shape using measurements made at fixed times?
Hint 2: Once you have measured the voltage at one instant, what number form must it be turned into so X and the fibre can handle it?
parts.proper_answer: The ADC samples the analogue signal at regular intervals and converts each sampled analogue value into a digital / binary number.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sampling the Wave**
Imagine freezing the microphone voltage at very rapid, equally spaced moments in time. That is sampling. The ADC measures the analogue voltage at each sampling instant.

Step 2: **Converting to Binary**
Each measured voltage is then quantised and coded as a binary number, for example an 8-bit number. That stream of binary numbers is the digital representation of the speech that can be sent via X and the optic fibre.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: The fibre loss and the signal-to-noise at the output are both given in dB - think about how the input power relates first to the output signal power, and then to the output noise power.
Hint 2: Work out the total loss along the 84 km fibre from the loss per km, then consider how dB values combine by addition when you chain ratios together.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Fibre Loss in dB**
Loss in a fibre grows with length, and dB values simply scale. Here: $$ \text{attenuation} = \text{length} \times \text{loss per km} $$ $$ \text{attenuation} = 84 \times 0.19 \approx 16\text{ dB} $$ This means the signal power at the output is 16 dB below the input power.

Step 2: **Add the Two dB Stages**
At the output, the signal is 28 dB above the noise: $$ 28 = 10\lg\left(\frac{P_{signal,out}}{P_{noise,out}}\right) $$ You want input power compared to output noise. In log units you just add: $$ 10\lg\left(\frac{P_{in}}{P_{noise,out}}\right) = 10\lg\left(\frac{P_{in}}{P_{signal,out}}\right) + 10\lg\left(\frac{P_{signal,out}}{P_{noise,out}}\right) $$ $$ = 16 + 28 = 44\text{ dB} $$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: conversion from dB to linear power
hints: Hint 1: You now know the power ratio in dB is 44 dB - recall the general link between a ratio in dB and the ratio of the two actual powers using log base 10.
Hint 2: Identify which power is on top: input power $9.7\text{ mW}$ is the larger power, noise power $P$ is the unknown smaller power, so set up $44 = 10\lg(9.7\times10^{-3}/P)$.
Hint 3: To isolate $P$, first divide by 10 to get $\lg(...)=4.4$, then use antilog $10^{4.4}$ and rearrange, remembering to keep the final answer in W.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the dB Definition**
For powers, the level in decibels is: $$ \text{ratio / dB} = 10\lg\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right) $$ Here $P_2$ is the input power and $P_1$ is the noise power at the output.

Step 2: **Substitute the Known Values**
Input power $9.7\text{ mW} = 9.7\times10^{-3}\text{ W}$ and ratio $=44\text{ dB}$: $$ 44 = 10\lg\left(\frac{9.7\times10^{-3}}{P}\right) $$ where $P$ is the noise power.

Step 3: **Solve for the Noise Power**
Divide by 10: $$ \lg\left(\frac{9.7\times10^{-3}}{P}\right) = 4.4 $$ Take antilogs: $$ \frac{9.7\times10^{-3}}{P} = 10^{4.4} $$ $$ P = \frac{9.7\times10^{-3}}{10^{4.4}} \approx 3.9\times10^{-7}\text{ W} $$ This tiny value makes sense because 44 dB is a power factor of about 25000.
